title: What If You Were in a COMA but Could Hear Everything?
description:
A storm, a blackout, a railing that isn't there. Glint, 19, wakes up in a coma: he can't move a finger, but he can hear everything. Doctors give the family forty-eight hours. Nan reads him the football scores. Kai confesses two secrets. And at three in the morning, a kind visitor from the museum leans over the bed and whispers something that proves the fall was no accident. The only way to tell anyone is real neuroscience: imagine playing tennis for YES, imagine walking through your house for NO.

If you were trapped in your own body and could hear everything, what would you want the people you love to say to you? Tell me in the comments 👇

CHAPTERS
0:00 Cold open: Forty-eight hours
0:30 The storm and the fall
1:20 The Rules: Glasgow Coma Scale and hidden awareness
2:16 Plus: Nan
2:49 Minus: "Can you hear me, love?"
3:18 Plus: Dr. Osei and the tennis test
4:03 Minus: Kai's secret
4:39 Minus: The 3 a.m. visitor
5:14 The Crisis: Forty-eight hours
6:44 The Solution: Tennis means yes
8:00 The Twist: Kai's notebook
8:49 Would you?

SOURCES
• Teasdale & Jennett, The Lancet (1974): the Glasgow Coma Scale (3 to 15; 8 or less is the usual coma threshold)
• Bodien et al., New England Journal of Medicine 391 (2024): hidden awareness ("cognitive motor dissociation") in about 1 in 4 patients with no behavioural response
• Owen et al., Science 313: 1402 (2006): a patient who seemed vegetative imagined tennis and walking through her house, with brain activity like healthy volunteers
• Monti et al., New England Journal of Medicine 362: 579 (2010): yes/no answers using tennis vs navigation imagery in fMRI
• Di et al., Neurology 68 (2007); Blundon et al., Scientific Reports 10 (2020): brain responses to voices and sound in unresponsive patients
• Pape et al., Neurorehabilitation and Neural Repair (2015): familiar family stories and faster recovery (small trial, 15 patients)
• Jean-Dominique Bauby, The Diving Bell and the Butterfly (1997): written by blinking one eyelid with a frequency-ordered alphabet
• NHS and Headway UK guidance on coma, talking to patients and post-traumatic amnesia
• Story is fiction: Glint's experience, Mr. Hale, the Kestrel Meteorite and the timings are made up; the science is real.
